measures: Florida's rolls are assessed on 1 January. The storm year's roll describes each house before the storm; the four rolls after it fall about 3, 15, 27, 39 months after a September landfall.

One minus the house's structure value on the first roll after the storm over its value on the storm year's roll, after the county's reassessment trend (the mode of the same ratio over the county's houses). Damaged: L of .25 or more. Destroyed: .50 or more, the 50% line of the federal substantial-damage rule.
Restored: structure value back to .90 of its pre-storm value after the county trend. Cleared: no structure on the roll. Rebuilt: a year built on or after the storm year.
The fraction of the pre-storm structure value regained, capped at 1.
On the storm year's roll: resident owner-occupant (an individual or trust with a homestead exemption), non-resident individual (an individual or trust without one), business entity.

Return: restored, the same owner name, the homestead exemption still on the roll. Owner change: a new owner name on any roll from the first after the storm; the deed month places a sale before or after restoration.
A tract with FEMA-verified real-property losses of at least 5 per 100 owner-occupied housing units (D).

The mean of two standardized tract measures: the share of the tract's owner registrants reporting homeowners or flood insurance, and the log of tract median household income. NFIP policies in force at landfall per 100 owner-occupied units give an independent measure.
Houses in storm-struck tracts whose owner had held them since two rolls before the storm, so a house bought shortly before the storm to be torn down does not count as storm damage.
models: Linear probability models with tract-by-season fixed effects: each house is compared only with houses of its own tract after the same storm. Standard errors clustered by county, tract clusters as a check.
Controls on the storm year's roll: structure value per square foot, land share of value, land value per square foot, house age, living area, mobile home, flood class, distance to the shore.
H1: among restored resident homes, owner change by s+3 (the third roll after the storm, about 27 months) on a loss of .50 or more against .25 to .50.
H2: among resident homes, damaged or not, return and owner change at s+2 (the second roll after the storm, about 15 months) on damage, damage × K, damage × flood zone and the loss bins.
H3: restoration at s+2 and s+3 on owner group, damage and their product, so the owner gap among damaged houses is read net of the same gap among undamaged houses.

The tests of H1 and H2 and their reading rules were written before the outcomes were examined. H3's rule, that the business gap be significant at both horizons, was missed at s+2, so H3 is reported as a description.

limits: Owner type is not random; comparisons within tract and season, loss bins, controls and the undamaged reference remove much of the selection, not all. Turnover is read as a pathway, never as a cause.
Capital is measured at the tract, not the house.
Repair-level restoration is measured with noise, worst in Lee County; the main estimates are shown without it.
The 2024 storms reach the second roll only on the 2026 Preliminary roll.
Learners trained on the 2016 to 2020 storms predict recovery after Ian and Idalia poorly, so the hypotheses are read from the statistical models, not from the learners.
